title: The inner light
hook: George Fox and the Quakers: there is that of God in everyone, found in silent waiting

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Brother Lawrence, and his omelet turned for the love of God. Your line was God among the pots.

A plain room, with wooden benches facing each other. No altar, no pulpit, no music. People come in and sit down. And then nothing happens. Nobody leads. Nobody speaks. Five minutes. Twenty. A cough, a creaking bench, a bird outside. Then, maybe, someone stands, says a few quiet sentences, and sits down again. More silence. In a silent Quaker meeting, that is what worship looks like. It began with a restless young man in England.

George Fox was born in 1624, in a time of civil war and religious turmoil in England. As a young man he was desperate for spiritual answers. He went from minister to minister, and none of them could help. Then, he wrote in his Journal, when all his hopes in people were gone, he heard a voice that said, in his own old English: "There is one, even Christ Jesus, that can speak to thy condition." His heart, he says, leapt for joy. Fox came to believe that God speaks directly to every person, not only through clergy or buildings. He pointed to the Gospel of John, which says of Christ: "That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world." Every person. Friends came to call this the inner light, or the light within. Fox's followers called themselves Friends; others nicknamed them Quakers. They gathered in silence and waited for that light to speak. In a letter from prison in 1656, Fox urged them to "walk cheerfully over the world, answering that of God in every one." Not only in the people who agree with you. In the jailer. The stranger. The enemy. Friends have traced some costly choices back to that conviction: work against slavery, prison reform, refusing to fight in wars. Today Quaker worship comes in different kinds. Some meetings still wait in silence. Others, in parts of Africa and the Americas, have pastors, hymns and sermons. Friends of both kinds speak of that of God in everyone.
screen: `SPEAK TO THY CONDITION.` · `THE TRUE LIGHT, WHICH LIGHTETH EVERY MAN.` · `SILENT WAITING.` · `THAT OF GOD IN EVERY ONE.`

segments.voice: Sit in silence with one other person if someone is near, or picture someone you know sitting across from you: no talking, no phones. Don't try to make anything happen; just wait. If a thought feels like light, hold it, and if it's only noise, let it pass.
Quakers. The nickname for Fox's Friends, who wait in silence for God's light within every person to speak.
Your line: that of God in everyone. Even in the people who annoy you. That's day two hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: In unprogrammed meetings, Quakers gather for worship in silence, speaking only when they feel led; in programmed meetings, found in parts of Africa and the Americas, they worship with pastors, hymns and sermons.

fork.setup: you're at a silent Quaker meeting. twenty minutes have passed and nobody has spoken. what do you do?
options: keep waiting; speak only if you feel led.

fork.reveal: the silence is the worship. Friends wait, and speak only when they sense the light moving them to.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice idea that everyone is basically good.
what it means: God's light reaches every person, so every person can be answered as someone God speaks to.
what a scholar hears: Fox's Journal (1647 experience); John 1:9 as the key verse; and 'answering that of God in every one' from his 1656 letter.
